name: Joule’s early heat equivalent
summary: Joule's first experimental estimate of how much mechanical work produces a given amount of heat, a scattered but early number linking the two.
description: Joule compared mechanical expenditure with heating in magneto-electric experiments, reporting an initial mean equivalent of 838 foot-pounds per pound of water warmed by one Fahrenheit degree, while acknowledging substantial scatter.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.

market.note: Commercial availability is not a milestone of a scientific knowledge result.

date.label: 1843 report
date.basis: July 1843 dated paper; August presentation and later 1843 serial publication, distinguished from the 1884 collected edition.

events.statement: Joule compared mechanical expenditure with heating in magneto-electric experiments, reporting an initial mean equivalent of 838 foot-pounds per pound of water warmed by one Fahrenheit degree, while acknowledging substantial scatter.
events.caveats: 838 is the historical reported estimate, not the accepted modern equivalent. The claim of reverse convertibility goes beyond a direct demonstration in every stated case.

evidence.locator: Collected pp. 156–158; conclusion, July signature and postscript; p. 156 visually inspected
evidence.supports: Initial numerical equivalent, acknowledged discrepancies, planned improved apparatus and water-friction comparison.

date.label: by August 1851
date.basis: The inspected English translation appearing in the August 1851 Philosophical Magazine cites Joule’s 1843 magneto-electric result; the relevant separate 1850 German installment was not inspected.

events.statement: By the August 1851 English translation, Clausius had acknowledged Joule’s 1843 magneto-electric determination in his heat–work analysis.
events.scope: Joule’s 1843 magneto-electric determination of the mechanical equivalent of heat.
events.caveats: Clausius gives a converted figure; numerical conventions and temperature references are not silently equated. The 1851 translation bounds this recognition from above; the relevant 1850 German installment was not inspected.

evidence.locator: Phil. Mag. series 4, vol. 2 no. 9, August 1851, printed p. 119 and footnote
evidence.supports: Clausius compares Joule’s magneto-electric result in converted units and cites the 1843 Phil. Mag. vol. 23 p. 441.

evidence.locator: First Memoir, printed pp. 15 and 68–69, including Joule note
evidence.supports: Cites Joule’s 1843 magneto-electric determination and its heat–work implications.

links.statement: In the later series 2 arrangement, Joule used the immersed rotating electromagnet with a newly built stationary inducing magnet to measure heating; he repeated that series with falling weights when estimating the 1843 heat equivalent.
links.scope: The revised series 2 configuration reported in 1843, not the initial engine-magnet setup.
links.alternatives: The postscript also reports fluid-friction experiments with a different apparatus.
links.caveats: The rotating component was reused but the stationary inducing magnet changed; the configurations remain separate.
links.timing: Both are dated by the report; apparatus use precedes the resulting analysis within that episode.

evidence.supports: Replacement of the original stationary inducing magnets, reused immersed rotating component, series 2 heating measurements and repetition with falling weights.

links.statement: Joule explicitly discussed Rumford’s cannon-friction experiment as a precedent consistent with heat generation rather than a change in metal heat capacity.
links.scope: 1843 paper postscript and its discussion of friction experiments.
links.alternatives: Joule also investigated electricity and fluid friction independently.
links.caveats: This is explicit engagement with a reported result, not proof that Rumford supplied Joule’s instrument design.

evidence.locator: Collected p. 157 postscript continuing onto p. 158
evidence.supports: Names Rumford and the cannon-boring interpretation directly.
